Osho — Facts and Teachings
===========================

Early Life and Background
-------------------------
Osho, born as Rajneesh Chandra Mohan Jain on 11 December 1931 in Kuchwada, a small village in Madhya Pradesh, India, was a spiritual teacher and philosopher who gained worldwide recognition. He was the eldest of eleven children born to a cloth merchant family. His parents were Babulal and Saraswati Jain. He spent his early childhood with his maternal grandparents, who gave him a great deal of freedom that he later credited with shaping his independent spirit.

Education and Academic Career
-----------------------------
Osho was a brilliant student and a natural debater. He studied philosophy at D.N. Jain College in Jabalpur and later completed his Master of Arts in Philosophy from the University of Sagar in 1957. After graduation, he was appointed as a professor of philosophy at the University of Jabalpur, where he taught for nine years from 1958 to 1966. He was known for his charismatic lectures and unconventional teaching style that challenged traditional beliefs.

Spiritual Awakening
-------------------
Osho claimed to have experienced spiritual enlightenment on 21 March 1953, at the age of 21, while sitting under a maulshree tree in the Bhanvartal Garden in Jabalpur. He described this experience as a profound dissolution of the ego and a merging with the universal consciousness. This date later became celebrated by his followers as "Enlightenment Day."

Philosophy and Teachings
------------------------
Osho's philosophy was a unique blend of Eastern mysticism and Western thought. He believed in the concept of "Zorba the Buddha," which combined the earthly enjoyment of life (like Zorba the Greek) with the spiritual awareness of the Buddha. His key teachings include:

1. Meditation as the core practice: Osho developed over 100 meditation techniques, including his famous "Dynamic Meditation," which involves stages of chaotic breathing, catharsis, jumping, silence, and celebration. He believed traditional sitting meditation was not suitable for the modern mind.

2. Living in the present moment: He taught that the past and future are illusions and that true freedom comes from being fully present in the "here and now."

3. Embracing contradictions: Osho often made seemingly contradictory statements intentionally, believing that truth cannot be captured in logical consistency. He wanted people to go beyond the rational mind.

4. Freedom from organized religion: He was a fierce critic of organized religion and institutional belief systems. He believed that spirituality is a personal journey, not something that can be institutionalized.

5. Celebration of life: Unlike many ascetic traditions, Osho encouraged his followers to celebrate life in all its forms — love, laughter, creativity, and even material comfort.

The Rajneesh Movement
---------------------
In 1966, Osho resigned from his teaching position and began traveling across India giving public talks. By 1970, he settled in Mumbai and started initiating followers, known as "neo-sannyasins," who wore orange robes and a mala (necklace) with his picture. In 1974, he established an ashram in Koregaon Park, Pune, which attracted thousands of visitors from around the world, especially from Europe and America.

Rajneeshpuram — The Oregon Experiment
--------------------------------------
In 1981, Osho moved to the United States and his followers purchased a 64,000-acre ranch in Wasco County, Oregon. They built a city called Rajneeshpuram, which had its own airport, shopping mall, dam, fire department, and public transport system. At its peak, the community had around 7,000 residents. The city faced significant conflicts with local residents and Oregon state authorities, leading to legal battles over land use, immigration fraud, and other issues. In 1985, Osho was arrested while reportedly trying to leave the country, pleaded guilty to immigration charges, and was deported from the United States.

Return to India and Later Years
-------------------------------
After being denied entry by 21 countries, Osho returned to his ashram in Pune, India, in 1987. He renamed himself "Osho" in 1989, a name derived from William James' term "oceanic experience." During his later years, he gave daily discourses and continued to develop new meditation techniques. His health declined significantly during this period — he claimed this was due to poisoning by US authorities during his brief imprisonment, though this was never independently confirmed.

Death and Legacy
----------------
Osho died on 19 January 1990, at the age of 58, at his ashram in Pune. His samadhi (memorial) at the ashram bears the inscription: "Osho — Never Born, Never Died, Only Visited this Planet Earth between December 11, 1931 and January 19, 1990."

After his death, the Pune ashram was renamed the "Osho International Meditation Resort" and continues to attract hundreds of thousands of visitors annually from over 100 countries. It offers various meditation programs, therapy groups, and creative workshops.

Controversies and Criticism
---------------------------
Osho remains one of the most controversial spiritual figures of the 20th century. He was known for his collection of 93 Rolls-Royce automobiles, his provocative statements about sex and religion, and the criminal activities carried out by some of his followers. Despite the controversies, his teachings on meditation, awareness, and individual freedom continue to influence millions of people worldwide. His approach to spirituality — irreverent, humorous, and deeply personal — set him apart from traditional spiritual teachers.

Number of Followers
-------------------
During his lifetime, Osho attracted followers from across the globe. It is estimated that he initiated over 200,000 neo-sannyasins. Today, his teachings continue to reach new audiences through books, online videos, and meditation centers in over 60 countries. The Osho International Meditation Resort in Pune receives approximately 200,000 visitors per year.

Impact on Modern Meditation
----------------------------
Osho had a significant impact on how meditation is practiced in the modern world. His Dynamic Meditation technique, which involves vigorous physical activity before silence, was designed specifically for people with "chattering minds" who found traditional sitting meditation difficult. Many contemporary mindfulness and meditation programs have been influenced by his approach of making meditation accessible and relevant to modern life.
